## Example

Use mobility $\mu>0$, stiffness $k>0$, and fixed bath temperature $T_b>0$. Under the adopted linear bath model, the stationary position spectrum has angular-frequency convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stationary Gaussian preparation of the specified linear model.

[F1] [[post-td-linear-ornstein-uhlenbeck-bath]]: its supplied center-of-mass data and constant velocity select one common rest chart throughout the modeled interval; $\gamma=\mu k$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$.

[F2] [[pthm-td-ornstein-uhlenbeck-thermal-fluctuations]]: $C(\tau)=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k)e^{-\mu k|\tau|}$ and the exact model spectrum is known.

## Verification

**Given:** $\gamma=\mu k>0$ and $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$.

1.1 Substituting $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$ and $\gamma=\mu k$ into the exact spectrum supplied by [F2] gives $S(\omega)=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\pi[(\mu k)^2+\omega^2])$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same supplier bound becomes $\operatorname{Var}(T^{-1}\int_0^T X_tdt)\le2k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\mu k^2T)$, which tends to zero as $T\to\infty$. Both formulas are conditional model predictions, not measurements. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

At a stipulated common $T,p$, let one mole of a component occupy phase $\alpha$ with molar volume $v_\alpha=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$ or phase $\beta$ with $v_\beta=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Consider a separated mixture of total amount $N=2\,\mathrm{mol}$ and total volume $V=5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}$; use the volume convention of [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and additivity of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Both phases are present, their molar volumes and the mixture totals are as in the Example, and volume and amount are additive for this separated compound.

[F1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: For one component, the phase amounts add to $N$, and the separated phase volumes add to $V$.

## Verification

1.1 Let $\lambda_\beta:=n_\beta/N$ and $\lambda_\alpha:=n_\alpha/N$. Positivity and amount additivity give $\lambda_\alpha+\lambda_\beta=1$, with both fractions in $(0,1)$. Volume additivity gives
$$
\bar v:=\frac VN=\lambda_\alpha v_\alpha+\lambda_\beta v_\beta.
$$
All terms have units $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Here $\bar v=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Solving the affine relation in step 1.1 yields
$$
\lambda_\beta=\frac{\bar v-v_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12,\qquad \lambda_\alpha=\frac{v_\beta-\bar v}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12.
$$
The fractions are positive and sum to one, so $n_\alpha=n_\beta=1\,\mathrm{mol}$ satisfies the given total amount and volume. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite integers, open coordinate domain, $C^1$ chemical-potential coordinate functions, coexistence equations, and nonsingular-minor assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative-matrix entries.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ map whose derivative has a specified invertible square minor has a local zero set that is a graph over the remaining coordinates, of dimension ambient dimension minus equation count.

[L2] [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]: finite sums and differences of $C^1$ real-valued maps are $C^1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $P\ge2$, $F$ has one scalar component for each pair $(i,\alpha)$ with $1\le i\le C$ and $2\le\alpha\le P$, so it has $q=C(P-1)$ components. Each is a difference of $C^1$ maps and therefore $F$ is $C^1$ on the open set $U$ by [F1, L2]. The assumed minor lets [L1] apply, giving local graph dimension $n-q$. Expanding $n=2+P(C-1)$ gives $n-q=2+PC-P-CP+C=C-P+2$. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra]

1.2 If $P=1$, no phase-equality equations are indexed because there is no $\alpha\ge2$. The local solution set is all of the open domain $U$, which has $n=2+(C-1)=C+1=C-P+2$ coordinates. [given, algebra]

2.1 In the reactive variant, each added affinity is a finite linear combination of $C^1$ coordinate functions and is therefore $C^1$ by [F1, L2]; the combined map has $q+R$ scalar equations. Its stated minor satisfies [L1], so the graph dimension is $n-q-R=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R=C-P+2-R$. Linear independence of the $\nu^r$ identifies $R$ distinct reaction directions, while the full-rank minor remains a separate necessary assumption on the equation derivatives. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $C=1$, $P=2$, and $R=0$. Fix $T_0=300\,\mathrm K$ and $p_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and take a common open chart around $(T_0,p_0)$. On it define the branch Gibbs potentials per mole
$$
g_1(T,p)=g_0-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_1(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,\qquad g_2(T,p)=g_0-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_2(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
where $g_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $s_0,c>0$ are in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_1,v_2>0$ are distinct molar volumes in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, and $\kappa>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. Set $G_i=n_i g_i$ with natural Gibbs assignments $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, and $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$; define $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. The derivative-defined chemical potentials are $\mu_i=g_i$, and they agree at $(T_0,p_0)$. This is a candidate equation-map solution, not a claim of entropy-maximizing coexistence.

The constructed branch's local physical state map is $\chi:(T,p,n)\mapsto(U,V,n)$ (using the positive amount and interior composition coordinates displayed here). On the inverse patch verified below, define its numerical domain $O_c=\Phi_c^{-1}(\chi(\mathcal O))$ and declare this patch to be the local model's $D_c$ patch, where $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n\,\mathrm{mol})$ is the unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Define the numerical entropy by $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$, with $S^{\rm SI}$ supplied by the Gibbs assignments through this inverse. Thus the displayed derivatives are derivatives in physical SI coordinates on $\Phi_c(O_c)$; the model patch is not an empirical claim about an independently specified material domain.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two Gibbs branches and the open $(T,p)$ chart described above, with $v_1\ne v_2$. The example is a conditional equation-map model, not an experimental claim.

[A1] The common positive-temperature, positive-pressure-or-real-pressure chart has no independent composition coordinates because $C=1$.

[A2] Adopted local Gibbs model: $G_i=n_i g_i$, $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-phase-dimension]]: For $C=1$, $P=2$, $R=0$, a coexistence-equation zero with a nonsingular derivative minor has local equation-set dimension $C-P+2=1$.

[F2] The model and calculation are only for a candidate equation-map solution; no stable or realized coexistence endpoint is assumed.

[L1] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: A $C^1$ map between open Euclidean sets with invertible derivative at a point has a local $C^1$ inverse there.

## Verification

1.1 From [A2], at $(T_0,p_0)$, $S_i=n_i s_0$, $V_i=n_i v_i$, $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$. Thus the $(T,p)$ derivative matrix of $(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed amount has determinant $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$, so [L1] supplies a valid local physical-coordinate chart. [given, A2, L1, algebra]

2.1 The only coexistence equation is $F(T,p):=g_2(T,p)-g_1(T,p)=(v_2-v_1)(p-p_0)=0$. It vanishes at the center and has $\partial_pF=v_2-v_1\ne0$, so the $1\times1$ minor is invertible. [given, A2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Here the ambient dimension is $n=2+P(C-1)=2$ and the equation count is $q=C(P-1)=1$. Applying [F1] gives local equation-set dimension $n-q=1$, exactly $C-P+2=1$. This verifies the regular equation-set rank calculation only. [F1, F2, A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Postulate

Adopt **C1 (equilibrium-join coherence)**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the joined state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each constituent, $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T x$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T y$, using the model’s declared nested-join identifications.

C1 is an additional postulate of this completed contact branch. The source’s Theorem 4.8 is stated with T1–T4; the local conditional calibrator route uses the constituent-to-join bridge in addition to the stronger T5 range assumption. Neither fact licenses deriving C1 from $u=u_i+u_j$, from T1–T4, or from transitivity alone. The displayed source supports the contact context, not the claim that its bare printed axioms already contain C1.

## Postulate

Adopt **T5 (universal thermal-equilibrium range)**: for every ordered pair of simple systems $i,j$, each state $x$ of $i$, and every work-coordinate point $v_j$ in the projection of the state domain of $j$, there is some state $y=(u_j,v_j)$ of $j$ with $x\sim_T y$, using [[def-td-thermal-join]].

This is a quantified existence assumption for a thermal-equilibrium partner at each permitted work coordinate. It does not define a numerical temperature, assert that all systems possess the same temperature range as a real apparatus, or supply a calibration map and its uncertainty.

## Example

Take finitely many tagged simple types $i$, each with positive dimensionless coordinates $u>0,v>0$ (numerical energy and work coordinates relative to fixed units). Choose constants $c_i,r_i>0$, reference values $u_{\star,i},v_{\star,i}>0$, and $b_i\in\mathbb R$, and define

$$s_i(u,v)=c_i\log\frac{u}{u_{\star,i}}+r_i\log\frac{v}{v_{\star,i}}+b_i.$$

For a scaled tag $t i$, set its coefficients to $tc_i,tr_i,tb_i$ and its reference coordinates to $t u_{\star,i},t v_{\star,i}$, so $s_{ti}(tu,tv)=t\,s_i(u,v)$. On finite separated compounds define the relation by nondecrease of the sum of the constituent entropies. For a thermal join of $i,j$, define the joined entropy at $(U,v_i,v_j)$ as the maximum of $s_i(u_i,v_i)+s_j(u_j,v_j)$ over $u_i,u_j>0$ with $u_i+u_j=U$, and define contact equilibrium by equality of the pair entropy with this maximum. For nested joins, use the same maximum construction recursively.

This formal model explicitly declares each equilibrium endpoint domain to be the stated positive numerical orthant, with endpoint coordinate map the identity and accessibility the entropy-sum relation above. Its fixed unit map assigns $U=u(1\,\mathrm J)$ and each work coordinate $W_a=v_aw_a$ for a fixed positive unit $w_a$; this bookkeeping supplies no material realization. Each primitive tag has a fixed formal composition, while the joined endpoint space is the positive orthant in summed energy and retained work coordinates with the summed composition. A scaled copy transports these coordinates and that composition and retains its distinct tag, exactly as in the declared join interface. This provides a nondegenerate consistency witness for the order, geometric, contact, T5, and C1 assumptions on this positive-coordinate family. It supplies no measured parameter values or empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive coordinates; fixed $c_i,r_i>0$, reference values and constants; tagged scaling as stated; accessibility is defined by entropy nondecrease; join entropy is the constrained maximum.

[F1] [[def-td-thermal-join]]: a join retains component work coordinates and sums the energy coordinate.

[F2] [[post-td-accessibility-a1-a6]]: A1–A6 are the order conditions to be checked for the example relation.

[F3] [[post-td-simple-system-geometric-axioms]]: A7 and S1–S3 are the geometric conditions to be checked.

[F4] [[post-td-thermal-join-axioms]]: T1–T4 are the contact conditions to be checked.

[F5] [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]] and [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]]: T5 and C1 are separate conditions to be checked.

[F6] [[thm-exponential-two-point-convexity]]: for $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $\exp((1-t)a+tb)\le(1-t)\exp(a)+t\exp(b)$; for $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $a=b$.

[F7] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, and $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$.

[F8] [[def-real-power]] and [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]: for $K>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $v^\alpha$ is differentiable for $v>0$ with derivative $\alpha v^{\alpha-1}$.

[F9] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if $g$ is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable inside, its endpoint slope equals $g'$ at some interior point.

## Verification
**Given:** [F1]–[F5] and the construction in the Example.

1.1 For $a,b>0$, apply [F6] to $\log a,\log b$, then use [F7] and monotonicity of $\log$, to obtain $\log((1-t)a+tb)\ge(1-t)\log a+t\log b$ for $0\le t\le1$. Apply this inequality to the energy ratios $u/u_{\star,i}$ and to the work ratios $v/v_{\star,i}$; multiplying by $c_i,r_i>0$ and adding $b_i$ proves concavity of $s_i$. This verifies the convex-combination accessibility condition. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, raising $u$ at fixed $v$ gives a strict successor, proving S1. [F3, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 The boundary equation $s_i(u',v')=s_i(u_x,v_x)$ rearranges to $u'=g(v')=K(v')^{-\alpha}$, where $K=u_xv_x^\alpha>0$ and $\alpha=r_i/c_i>0$. By [F8], $g'=-\alpha K(v')^{-\alpha-1}$ and $g''=\alpha(\alpha+1)K(v')^{-\alpha-2}>0$. Thus $g'$ is increasing by [F9]. For $v'\ne v_x$, the mean value theorem on the interval between them and the monotonicity of $g'$ give $g(v')\ge g(v_x)+g'(v_x)(v'-v_x)$: when $v'<v_x$, both the derivative comparison and the sign of $v'-v_x$ reverse. Hence the forward sector $u'\ge g(v')$ lies above the tangent support $u'-u_x+(r_i u_x/(c_iv_x))(v'-v_x)=0$. A vertical line cannot support this sector because its work coordinate varies on both sides at an interior boundary point. If a nonvertical line with slope parameter $q$ supports there, its inequality on graph points gives $g(v')-g(v_x)+q(v'-v_x)\ge0$ for both signs of $v'-v_x$; dividing by that difference and taking limits forces $q=-g'(v_x)$. This proves uniqueness and gives $P_i=r_i u_x/(c_iv_x)$. On any closed rectangle with $u,\tilde u\le u_1$ and $v,\tilde v\ge v_0>0$, $|u/v-\tilde u/\tilde v|\le |u-\tilde u|/v_0+u_1|v-\tilde v|/v_0^2$, so the slope is locally Lipschitz. The graph over $v'>0$ is arcwise connected, proving S3. [F3, F8, F9, algebra]

1.3 Put $C=c_i+c_j$. For any split $u_i+u_j=U$, [F6] with weights $c_i/C,c_j/C$, followed by [F7], gives $$\frac{c_i}{C}\log\frac{u_i}{c_i}+\frac{c_j}{C}\log\frac{u_j}{c_j}\le\log\frac{U}{C},$$ with equality exactly when $u_i/c_i=u_j/c_j$. Since $u_i+u_j=U$, that equality forces the unique split $u_i=c_iU/C,\ u_j=c_jU/C$. Multiply by $C$ and add the constants $c_i\log(c_i/u_{\star,i})+c_j\log(c_j/u_{\star,j})+b_i+b_j+r_i\log(v_i/v_{\star,i})+r_j\log(v_j/v_{\star,j})$; the resulting inequality is exactly the pair entropy bounded by its value at that split. This proves attainment of the join maximum, T1, and reversible join splitting. For the equal-state scaled split, tagged extensivity gives $s_{ti}(tu,tv)=t s_i(u,v)$ and $s_{(1-t)i}((1-t)u,(1-t)v)=(1-t)s_i(u,v)$, so both sides have equal entropy and the other T2 clause holds. The binary join entropy is $C\log U+r_i\log v_i+r_j\log v_j+C_{ij}$ for a constant $C_{ij}$; its energy-to-coefficient ratio is $U/C=u_i/c_i=u_j/c_j$ at the maximizing split. [F1, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 On each finite product the relation compares finite real entropy sums. Reflexivity and transitivity follow from the real order; adding the same spectator adds the same number to both sides; positive scaling multiplies the sums by a positive coefficient; and reversible splitting preserves the extensive sum. If $A+\epsilon_nZ_0\prec B+\epsilon_nZ_1$, then $s(A)-s(B)\le\epsilon_n(s(Z_1)-s(Z_0))$. Taking $n\to\infty$ yields $s(A)\le s(B)$ and hence $A\prec B$. This verifies the six adopted order conditions. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a single system the entropy has the displayed logarithmic form. If a nested join has energy coefficient $C$ and is joined with a system of coefficient $c>0$, the maximum calculation of step 1.3 gives the unique maximizing split at equal energy-to-coefficient ratios; substitution adds $c$ to the energy coefficient and adds the new work term. Induction over the finite joins therefore gives coefficient $C=\sum_k c_k$ and entropy $C\log U+\sum_k r_k\log v_k+C_0$ for the positive work coordinates $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$. Its boundary is $U=g(v)=K\prod_k v_k^{-\alpha_k}$ with $\alpha_k=r_k/C>0$. Direct differentiation gives, for any vector $h$, $$D^2g(v)[h,h]=g(v)\left[\left(\sum_k\alpha_k\frac{h_k}{v_k}\right)^2+\sum_k\alpha_k\left(\frac{h_k}{v_k}\right)^2\right]\ge0.$$ Thus along each segment in the positive work orthant, the derivative of $g$ is nondecreasing by [F9], and the mean value theorem gives $g(v')\ge g(v)+\nabla g(v)\cdot(v'-v)$. The forward sector $U\ge g(v)$ lies above this tangent support; uniqueness follows by applying the support inequality to graph points in each direction $h$ and $-h$, which forces the support functional to equal $\nabla g(v)$. Its finite slope components are $P_k=r_kU/(Cv_k)$; on rectangles bounded away from all coordinate axes, the quotient estimate from step 1.2 applies to each component and proves local Lipschitz regularity. The positive orthant and its graph are arcwise connected. Increasing $U$ gives S1, and the coordinatewise concavity argument of step 1.1 gives the convex-combination accessibility condition. Hence each join satisfies the same simple-system geometry. [F3, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.3 Thermal equilibrium is equality of the positive ratios $u_i/c_i$ and $u_j/c_j$ by the unique maximum in step 1.3. Equality is transitive, proving T3. For any state $(u,v)$ choose $0<v_-<v<v_+$; strict increase of entropy with $v$ gives $(u,v_-)\prec\prec(u,v)\prec\prec(u,v_+)$, while the outer states have equal $u/c_i$. This proves T4. [F4, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Given any $u_i>0$ and any $v_j>0$, choose $u_j=c_j u_i/c_i$; this verifies T5. For an equilibrated pair, step 1.3 gives $(u_i+u_j)/(c_i+c_j)=u_i/c_i=u_j/c_j$. In a nested join of the joined type with constituent $i$, the pair is therefore at the maximizing split by the same two-factor calculation of step 1.3, so the joined state is thermally equivalent to $i$; replacing $i$ by $j$ proves the second equivalence and C1. [F5, step 1.3, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The coefficients are chosen mathematical parameters. Their existence checks compatibility of the postulates but does not report measurements, determine SI entropy units, or prove the assumptions for a real substance.

## Statement

Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. Suppose $V\subseteq\mathbb R^s$ is open, $n_*:=n^0+\nu\xi_*\in V$, $\Phi:V\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at $n_*$, and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$ near $\xi_*$. For each $j$, let $e_j\in\mathbb R^s$ have coordinate $1$ in position $j$ and $0$ in every other position; define $\mu_j:=D\Phi(n_*)e_j$. Then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite stoichiometric matrix, initial amounts, feasible extent set, Euclidean convergence, and differentiability/convexity hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]: differentiability at $\xi_*$ gives $f(\xi_*+w)=f(\xi_*)+Df(\xi_*)w+o(\|w\|_2)$ as $w\to0$.

[F2] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: convexity of $U$ and the affine inequalities defining $\mathcal F$ keep every segment between feasible points in $\mathcal F\cap U$.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its total derivatives.

[F4] [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]: a real-valued function is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for points in its convex domain and $t\in[0,1]$.

[F5] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]: a finite-dimensional linear map is bounded and therefore continuous.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$, and choose sequences $t_k,h_k$ from its definition. For each active $j\in J$, feasibility gives $0+t_k(\nu h_k)_j\ge0$, hence $(\nu h_k)_j\ge0$. Since [F5] makes the finite matrix map continuous, $h_k\to h$ implies $\nu h_k\to\nu h$, so $(\nu h)_j\ge0$. This proves one inclusion. [F5, given, algebra]

## Statement

Let an admitted refrigerator cycle in the sense of [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]] operate between fixed ideal-bath temperatures $0<T_c<T_h$, extract $Q_c>0$ from the cold bath, reject $Q_h>0$ to the hot bath, and consume $W_{\mathrm{in}}>0$. Define its cooling coefficient of performance by $\mathrm{COP}_R=Q_c/W_{\mathrm{in}}$. Then
$
\mathrm{COP}_R\le\frac{T_c}{T_h-T_c}.
$
Equality holds exactly when the total entropy change of the isolated compound is zero. A reversible cycle in the stated boundary model saturates the bound; no converse about reversibility is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A cyclic working system with $0<T_c<T_h$, $Q_c>0$, $Q_h>0$, $W_{\mathrm{in}}>0$, no unlisted transfers, and the full working system, baths, and work store inside the declared isolated compound.

[F1] [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]]: In refrigerator mode $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=W_{\mathrm{in}}$, the cold and hot bath energy changes are $-Q_c$ and $+Q_h$, their endpoint entropy changes are $-Q_c/T_c$ and $+Q_h/T_h$, and the work store supplies this work with $\Delta E_w=-W_{\mathrm{in}}$ and zero entropy change. The full compound has the admitted equilibrium endpoint record and additive entropy split required by the definition.

[F2] [[post-td-first-law-energy]]: For an admitted closed fixed-constitution process with zero endpoint changes in separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-potential energies, $\Delta U=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$.

[F3] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: For an admitted isolated compound process with equilibrium endpoints and the declared additive total entropy, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$; an admitted reversible operation has $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** The fixed-bath cycle hypotheses in the Statement and the heat/work signs in [F1].

1.1 The working system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$. Applying [F2] with [F1] gives $0=Q_c-Q_h+W_{\mathrm{in}}$, hence $Q_h=Q_c+W_{\mathrm{in}}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The cold bath loses $Q_c$, the hot bath gains $Q_h$, and their entropy slopes are constant. Thus their entropy changes are $-Q_c/T_c$ and $Q_h/T_h$. The working system and work store have zero entropy change, so [F3] gives
$
-\frac{Q_c}{T_c}+\frac{Q_h}{T_h}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0.
$
[given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $T_c,T_h>0$, step 1.2 gives $Q_h\ge Q_cT_h/T_c$. Substituting $Q_h=Q_c+W_{\mathrm{in}}$ from step 1.1 yields
$
W_{\mathrm{in}}\ge Q_c\frac{T_h-T_c}{T_c}.
$
[given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Divide by $W_{\mathrm{in}}>0$ and use $T_h-T_c>0$ to obtain $\mathrm{COP}_R\le T_c/(T_h-T_c)$. Equality is equivalent to $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$; a reversible cycle has this property by [F3]. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

- If energy exchange is permitted, $T_A=T_B$.
- If volume exchange is permitted, then $p_A/T_A=p_B/T_B$; if energy exchange is also permitted, this gives $p_A=p_B$.
- If species $j$ can be exchanged, then $\mu_{A,j}/T_A=\mu_{B,j}/T_B$; if energy exchange is also permitted, this gives $\mu_{A,j}=\mu_{B,j}$.

The pressure equality concerns the derivative-defined pressures of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. It is equality of mechanical piston pressures only when the coupling of [[post-td-mechanical-conjugate-identification]] applies. A retained volume or species constraint supplies no corresponding equality.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two named subsystems in independent separated states, fixed total coordinates, an explicitly declared feasible set $\mathcal F$, an attained global entropy-maximizing equilibrium point interior to every exchange direction used, $C^2$ entropy on the local charts, $S_{U}>0$, and SI coordinates. [A1] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]: For a stable equilibrium of the declared isolated compound, the model adopts an attained global maximum of the summed entropy on the exact feasible endpoint set. It assumes attainment; it proves no dynamics or uniqueness.

[F2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: On the selected smooth single-phase charts the entropy has finite $C^2$ derivatives and $S_U>0$, and independent separated constituents have additive entropy and the declared additive extensive coordinates.

[F3] [[def-td-thermal-contact-constraints]]: A diathermal contact permits thermal energy transfer between constituents while forbidding matter transfer and mechanical or composition work across that contact. Here it supports the energy-exchange variation only; [F1] and the stated bilateral-feasibility hypothesis govern the other named exchange channels.

[F4] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: Each $D_{c_i}$ uses dimensionless coordinates, and its physical chart is the image under $\Phi_{c_i}$; the entropy on physical tuples is the composition with $\Phi_{c_i}^{-1}$. The derivative identities are $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$, $S_{i,V}=p_i/T_i$, and $S_{i,n_j}=-\mu_{i,j}/T_i$, with other physical coordinates fixed.

[F5] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: The coordinates $U,V,n_j$ use joules, cubic metres, and moles; $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ in pascals, and $\mu_j$ in joules per mole.

[A2] [[post-td-mechanical-conjugate-identification]]: For the declared quasistatic frictionless piston, derivative pressure equals force per area and $\delta W_{\mathrm{on}}=-p\,dV$. This is an adopted coupling, not a mathematical consequence.

[L1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: For differentiable maps between open Euclidean sets, the derivative of a composition is the composition of the derivatives. This is the mathematical chain rule used to differentiate entropy along each feasible one-parameter exchange.

## Proof

1.1 For energy exchange choose an arbitrary sufficiently small $h$ joules and the feasible physical-coordinate curves $z_A(t)=(U_A^*+t h,V_A^*,n_A^*)$, $z_B(t)=(U_B^*-t h,V_B^*,n_B^*)$ for $t$ near $0$. Their state-domain coordinates are $\Phi_{c_A}^{-1}(z_A(t))$ and $\Phi_{c_B}^{-1}(z_B(t))$; openness of the physical charts and the bilateral-feasibility hypothesis make both signs locally feasible. By [A1], $g(t):=S_A(z_A(t))+S_B(z_B(t))$ has a local maximum at $0$; [F1] and [F3] specify that this thermal energy exchange is allowed. For $t>0$, $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le0$; for $t<0$, the same quotient is $\ge0$. Its derivative exists by [F2], so the two one-sided limits force $g'(0)=0$. The chain rule [L1] gives $g'(0)=h(S_{A,U}-S_{B,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{A,U}=S_{B,U}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, L1, construct]

2.1 By [F4], $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$ for $i=A,B$. The temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of their reciprocals gives $T_A=T_B$. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

When energy exchange is also permitted, step 2.1 gives $T_A=T_B>0$, hence $p_A=p_B$. By [A2], this is equality of the two derivative pressures with their respective mechanical piston pressures whenever that coupling applies to each subsystem. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 If species $j$ is permitted to cross the partition, hold other coordinates fixed and vary $n_{A,j}(t)=n_{A,j}^*+t q$, $n_{B,j}(t)=n_{B,j}^*-t q$ for a sufficiently small nonzero mole increment $q$. Both signs are feasible by hypothesis, so the same derivative argument as in step 1.1 gives $S_{A,n_j}=S_{B,n_j}$. By [F4], $-\mu_{A,j}/T_A=-\mu_{B,j}/T_B$; when energy exchange is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures and hence $\mu_{A,j}=\mu_{B,j}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

[given, F1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Remark

**Scope.**

Use the fields and local-equilibrium regime of [[rem-td-local-equilibrium-branch]]. A Fourier heat-transport model may postulate

$$\mathbf j_Q(\mathbf x,t)=-K(\mathbf x,t)\nabla T(\mathbf x,t),$$

where $\mathbf j_Q:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is a continuous heat-energy flux field in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and $K:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is a declared conductivity tensor with units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. In an isotropic model $K=\kappa I_3$ with $\kappa\ge0$. A diffusion model may separately postulate $\mathbf j_n=-D\nabla n$, where number density $n:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, number flux $\mathbf j_n:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $D$ is a declared scalar or tensor in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

These are constitutive choices for specified material, geometry, regime, field regularity and boundary conditions. A collision invariant in a kinetic model is a quantity preserved by each allowed collision. Near-equilibrium linear response, a dilute-gas Boltzmann model, a relaxation-time approximation, and a quantum transport model have different hypotheses and coefficient definitions. The relaxation-time approximation can fail to preserve collision invariants; a coefficient derived in one approximation is not thereby universal. Onsager reciprocity is a relation among linear-response coefficients under a specified microscopic time-reversal and conjugate-force convention; this remark does not assert it without those hypotheses. Microscopic calculations and measurements may determine or test coefficients for a specified model and material, but neither the equilibrium entropy postulates nor dimensional consistency alone determine them.

Any heat equation or transport conclusion additionally needs the relevant conservation balance, sources or work terms, constitutive relation, initial data and boundary conditions. No such evolution equation, Onsager relation, or transport coefficient is proved or adopted by this remark.

$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]]: for differentiable positive $Z$, $(\log Z)'=Z'/Z$.

**Given:** The finite canonical model and its fixed energy values.

$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent. The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. This lemma is a deterministic tail estimate; it uses no superstability or thermodynamic-limit conclusion.

**Given:** $d,R_0,\psi$ as in the Statement.

Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. ## Statement

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define

$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$

## Statement

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$. Then
$$1\leq\Xi_L(a,\beta)\leq\exp(ae^{\beta B}L^d),\qquad p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(a,\beta)$$
exists and is finite. This theorem assumes only stability and the decreasing integrable two-sided tail in regularity; it does not assert canonical fixed-density convergence, periodic-boundary equality, or arbitrary-region limits.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Dimension $d\geq1$, a stable regular pair potential, its stability constant $B$, and fixed numerical length and energy units.

[A1] Stability means $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration, and the grand partition uses the $1/N!$ normalization in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: for some nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi$ and $R_0<\infty$, $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$, with finite weighted integral $\int_{R_0}^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}dr$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: $\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g)$ and there are gaps $g(\ell)$ with $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$ and $(\ell/g(\ell))^d\eta(g(\ell))\to0$.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: $|[0,L)^d|=L^d$ and finite product Lebesgue measure gives $|([0,L)^d)^N|=L^{dN}$.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], and [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]: the nonnegative exponential series sums to $e^x$, $0!=1$, and nonnegative grand terms may be split into a finite partial sum and its tail.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative sums and product integrals factor over finitely many disjoint regions.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A stable regular pair potential, $\beta>0$, its free-cube canonical partition functions, and the exact entropy/rate conventions above.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugation]]: a proper closed convex function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space equals its biconjugate under the stated extended-real conventions.

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

Taking the supremum over interior densities gives the lower bound. The vacuum term $Z(L,0)=1$ gives the value $0$ at density zero. Endpoint values are limits from the interior by their definition, so they do not enlarge the supremum. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Put $q=e^{\alpha+\beta B}$. For each $N\geq0$, stability and the box-volume formula give $e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Choose $K>eq+1$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Choose maximizing retained particle numbers and a subsequence with $N_L/L^d\to\rho\in[0,K]$; nested-interval bisection on the compact interval $[0,K]$ supplies the subsequence. At $\rho=0$, stability gives upper rate at most $0=F_\beta(0)$. If $u$ is a finite upper endpoint and $b(u)>-\infty$, mix a preparation approaching $b(u)$ with an interior preparation of density $r<u$, in slab fractions $1-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. The exact packing inequality in [F1] gives $F_\beta((1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon r)\geq(1-\epsilon)b(u)+\epsilon b(r).$ As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the left side tends to the assigned interior endpoint limit; hence $b(u)\leq F_\beta(u)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The extension $F_\beta$ is proper, upper-semicontinuous and concave. It is finite and concave on its open effective interior by [F1], hence continuous there. The endpoint convention is needed for closedness; it asserts no finite-volume endpoint realization. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis supplies the uniform cell-occupation bound used below; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Use the half-open unit-cell partition $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$ from [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]] and first take a finite union $\mathcal R$ of these cells. Let $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$ be the unnormalized positional sector measure whose $N$-point part is $z^N/N!$ times product Lebesgue measure, and let $\mu_{\mathcal R}$ have density $e^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{free}}}/\Xi_{\mathcal R}$ relative to $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$. By [L1] and Tonelli [F5],
$$E N_i^2=E N_i+E[N_i(N_i-1)] \leq \xi |C_i\cap\mathcal R|+\xi^2|C_i\cap\mathcal R|^2 \leq M:=\xi+\xi^2.$$
This gives a uniform second-moment bound for every unit cell in every such region. [F1, F3, F5, L1, algebra]

2.1 For each $\Omega_k$, let $\mathcal R_k$ be the union of unit cells meeting $\Omega_k$. Then $\Xi_{\Omega_k}\leq\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}$ by domain monotonicity, and $|\mathcal R_k|/|\Omega_k|\to1$ by the van Hove boundary condition. Put $J_0=\lceil R_0+2\rceil$, where $R_0$ is the regular-tail cutoff in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and choose $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(J_0-1)\}$. For $j\in\mathbb Z^d$, define $\kappa_j=M_0$ when $|j|_\infty<J_0$ and $\kappa_j=\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ otherwise. If two particles occupy cells with offset $j$, their negative pair energy is bounded by $\kappa_j$: for near offsets, stability on a two-point configuration gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$, and for far offsets the regularity envelope applies. Also $\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Partition the cells of $\mathcal R_k$ into boxes $B$ of $\ell$ unit cells per side and, for each occupied cell $i$, set $e_i=\sum_{j:\,B(j)\neq B(i)}\kappa_{i-j}$. The negative cross-box energy obeys $W^-\leq\sum_i e_iN_i^2$, by $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$ and summation over ordered cross-box cell pairs. Step 1.1 gives $E W^-\leq M\sum_i e_i$, so Markov's inequality shows $W^-\leq2M\sum_i e_i$ with probability at least $1/2$ (with probability one if the sum vanishes). On this event $H_{\mathrm{total}}\geq H_{\mathrm{in}}-2M\sum_i e_i$, where $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the sum of within-box energies. Therefore
$$\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}/2\leq e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\prod_B\Xi_{\mathcal R_k\cap B}.$$
Indeed, $\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}\mu_{\mathcal R_k}(E)=\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{total}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$; bound this by $e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{in}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$, then factor the latter integral by boxes. Each unrestricted partial-box partition is at most the full $\ell$-cube partition. For one full box, put $E_\ell=\sum_{i\in B,j\notin B}\kappa_{i-j}$. For fixed $R$, cells within distance $R$ of the boundary contribute at most $O_R(\ell^{d-1})\sum_j\kappa_j$, while every other cell contributes at most $\ell^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\kappa_j$. Thus $E_\ell/\ell^d\to0$, by first letting $\ell\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$. Consequently
$$\limsup_k|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k} \leq\ell^{-d}\bigl[\log\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}+2\beta M E_\ell\bigr].$$
Let $\ell\to\infty$ and use [F4]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the lower bound, put $q=ze^{\beta B}$ and choose $K>eq+1$. For integer core side $\ell\geq1$, let $n_\ell$ be an integer with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$ and set $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}z^NZ(\Lambda_\ell,N;\beta)$. The stability tail estimate in the proof of [F4] gives $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}(z,\beta)$. Fix $g>2R_0$ and retain every complete $(\ell+g)$-tile whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. By [F2], the retained count $M_k$ divided by $|\Omega_k|$ tends $(\ell+g)^{-d}$. Each core has at most $(K+1)\ell^d$ particles. If two tile indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, their core points are separated by at least $mg$; hence the positive cross energy per core is at most
$$C_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Summing over cores, using the exact ordered-label assignment count to cancel the global $N!$, and discarding negative cross energy gives
$$\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta D_{k,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^{M_k},\qquad \frac{D_{k,\ell,g}}{|\Omega_k|}\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)+o_k(1).$$
First let $k\to\infty$. Then choose $g=g(\ell)$ from [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]] and let integer $\ell\to\infty$; $g/\ell\to0$, the packing fraction tends one, $(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)\to0$, and $\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$. The resulting liminf is at least the cube pressure [F4]. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the potential of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] is stable and regular. In addition, assume either (i) $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and nonincreasing, $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$, and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; or (ii) there is a hard-core radius $r_h>0$ such that $\phi(x)=+\infty$ whenever $|x|_\infty<r_h$. Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}h(N_{C_i}(\omega))-bN(\omega).$$
The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell. This is stronger than ordinary superstability and is not inferred from stability or regularity alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Stability, regularity, the unit-cell partition, and one of the two positive-core alternatives.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: if $H_\phi\geq-BN$, applying stability to a two-point configuration gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$ for every nonzero separation; regularity supplies an integrable lower-tail envelope.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: the integrable envelope gives a finite lattice sum outside any sufficiently large fixed gap.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Write $N_i=N_{C_i}(\omega)$. The negative part of each pair potential is bounded both by $2B$, where $B$ is the stability constant of $\phi$, and, at large separation, by the lower-regular envelope. Set $\Psi_j$ to a finite constant on the finitely many near-cell offsets and to the envelope evaluated at $|j|_\infty-1$ on the remaining offsets. The shell count $|\{j:|j|_\infty=m\}|\leq c_dm^{d-1}$ and the cell-envelope conclusion of [F2] give $\sum_j\Psi_j<\infty$. Since $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$, the total negative pair contribution is at most $C\sum_iN_i^2$ for a finite $C$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 In case (i), choose an integer $k_0\geq2$ with $1/(k_0-1)\leq r_1$. Then $\chi(1/k)$ and $\chi(1/(k-1))$ are both defined for every $k\geq k_0$. Partition one unit cell into $k^d$ half-open cubes of side $1/k$, put $\chi_k=\chi(1/k)$, and $\Delta\chi_k=\chi_k-\chi_{k-1}\geq0$. If the cell contains $N$ points, the identity $\sum_jn_j^2-N=2\sum_j\binom{n_j}{2}$ and nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_j-N/k^d)^2$ give at least $\frac12(N^2/k^d-N)$ same-subcube pairs at scale $k$. A fixed pair counted at scale $k$ has separation $s<1/k$, hence $k<1/s$; summing its nonnegative weights over all scales where it is counted is at most $\sum_{k=k_0}^{\lfloor1/s\rfloor}\Delta\chi_k\leq\chi(s)$. Thus the positive core energy in the cell dominates the sum of these weighted pair counts. With $K_N=\lfloor(N/2)^{1/d}\rfloor$, each $k\leq K_N$ satisfies $N^2/k^d-N\geq N^2/(2k^d)$, so the core energy is at least $$ \frac{N^2}{4}\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N}\frac{\Delta\chi_k}{k^d}. $$ Summation by parts writes the coefficient as an initial constant plus $\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N-1}\chi_k(k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d})$; and $k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d}\geq d/(2^{d+1}k^{d+1})$. The series $\sum_k\chi(1/k)k^{-d-1}$ diverges: on dyadic intervals $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, monotonicity bounds the integral above by $C_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$, while the corresponding block $2^{j+1}\leq k<2^{j+2}$ contributes at least $c_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$ to that series. The divergent core integral therefore forces the displayed coefficient to tend to infinity. [F1, algebra, construct]

2.1 In case (i), sum the cell core bound from step 1.2 and subtract the negative-pair bound from step 1.1. The resulting coefficient of $N_i^2$ tends to infinity with $N_i$. Above a finite threshold it dominates $2CN_i^2$; below that threshold its possible negative remainder is bounded by a constant times $N_i$. Taking $h(N)$ to be half the positive cell lower bound above the threshold and zero below it gives a nondecreasing extended-valued function with $h(N)/N^2\to\infty$ and $H_\phi\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 In case (ii), choose $k$ with $1/k<r_h$ and partition every unit cell into $k^d$ subcubes. A finite-energy configuration has at most one point in each subcube, so $N_i\leq k^d$ for every $i$. Define $h(N)=0$ for $N\leq k^d$ and $h(N)=+\infty$ for $N>k^d$. If any cell exceeds this occupancy, the configuration has a forbidden pair and $H_\phi=+\infty$; otherwise stability gives $H_\phi\geq-BN=\sum_i h(N_i)-BN$. This proves the hard-core alternative. [F1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume a stable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the genuine finite-valued positive-core condition of [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for some $r_0>0$, a nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_0]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_0$ and $\int_0^{r_0}\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. Let $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, $V_n=(2n+1)^d$, $C_i=i+[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)^d$, and $\mathcal C_{\rm lf}$ be the set of locally finite simple configurations $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For $\omega=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)$, write $H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. For $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, let $\zeta_n^{\rm out}=\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n$ and define the finite-volume boundary Hamiltonian
$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$
The exterior series has finite negative part by the proof below; its extended value may be $+\infty$, with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Define
$$Z_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_{n,\zeta}(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta).$$
For fixed $z,\beta>0$ and $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure with this exterior pair energy satisfies
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\zeta\in\Omega(t)}\left|\frac1{V_n}\log\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)-p(z,\beta)\right|=0,$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube pressure from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The exterior configuration is restricted to the stated fixed square-count class; no volume-filling external field is included. The conclusion is conditional on the genuine positive core and does not infer it from superstability alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive divergent core, regular far tail, fixed $z,\beta>0$, and a fixed finite tempering constant $t$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: stability gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$ for every nonzero separation, and the far pair interaction is bounded in absolute value by a decreasing integrable envelope $\psi$ outside some radius $R_0$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: the cell envelope is summable, and the diagonal tail choice has $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and $(\ell/g(\ell))^d\eta(g(\ell))\to0$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for the genuine core there is an increasing finite-valued $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,\infty)$ with $h(0)=0$, $h(m)/m^2\to\infty$, and $H\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$ on unit cells. [F4] [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]: all perturbed free-cube grand pressures at positive activity and inverse temperature exist and are finite.

[F5] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: Hölder’s inequality gives convexity of finite-volume log partition functions in inverse temperature and log activity.

[L1] Ruelle's tempered-boundary estimates apply to superstable, lower-regular interactions with the stated square-count exterior class; the full source proof and exact hypotheses were read. The near/far estimate used below is written explicitly in the proof.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Put $S_n=\{i\in\mathbb Z^d:|i|_\infty\leq n\}$, $v_n=|S_n|=V_n$, $N_i(\omega)=|\omega\cap C_i|$, $T_n(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}N_i(\omega)^2$, and $T_n^h(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}h(N_i(\omega))$. Choose $m_0\geq\lceil R_0+1\rceil$ and $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(m_0-1)\}$. Set $\gamma_m=M_0$ for integers $m<m_0$ and $\gamma_m=\psi(m-1)$ for $m\geq m_0$. Then $\gamma$ is nonincreasing, dominates the negative part at every cell offset, dominates $|\phi|$ at offsets $m\geq m_0$, and $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Let $\Delta_m=\gamma_m-\gamma_{m+1}\geq0$ and $v_m=(2m+1)^d$. Since $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$, Tonelli gives $\sum_m\Delta_m v_m=\sum_j\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$. Thus $\delta_k:=\frac12\sum_{m\geq k}\Delta_m v_m\to0$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$ and any $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, the long-offset cell sum satisfies
$$\sum_{i\in S_n,\ j\in\mathbb Z^d:\,|i-j|_\infty\geq k}\gamma_{|i-j|_\infty}N_i(\omega)N_j(\zeta)\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_n(\omega)+2^dtV_n\bigr).$$
Indeed, expand $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$ and enlarge the offset set in the $m$th term to $j\in S_m+i$. With
$$S_{n,m}(\zeta)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}N_j(\zeta)^2\,\#\{i\in S_n:j\in S_m+i\},$$
the inequality $ab\leq(a^2+b^2)/2$ bounds that term by $\frac12\Delta_m(v_mT_n+S_{n,m})$. The multiplicity is at most $\min(v_n,v_m)$ and vanishes unless $j\in S_{n+m}$, so $S_{n,m}\leq\min(v_n,v_m)t v_{n+m}\leq2^dtv_nv_m$. Summing proves the estimate. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 Set $g(r)=r\sqrt{h(r)}$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$ and $g^*(s)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb N_0}\{rs-g(r)\}$. Then $g(r)/r^2\to\infty$ and $g(r)/h(r)\to0$, so $g^*(s)/s^2\to0$: for each $a>0$, eventually $g(r)\geq r^2/(4a)$, and completing the square gives $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$. Also $rs\leq g(r)+g^*(s)$. For a fixed $k\geq m_0$, every near cross pair has its inside cell in $S_n\setminus S_{n-k}$ and its exterior cell in $S_{n+k}\setminus S_n$; its negative energy is at most $M_0$. Counting the finitely many offsets of size below $k$, for every $a>0$ we obtain
$$W^-_{\rm near}\leq C_k\left(aT_n^h+C_a|S_n\setminus S_{n-k}|+atv_{n+k}+C_a|S_{n+k}\setminus S_n|\right).$$
Here $g(r)\leq ah(r)+C_a$ and $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$ were used, with $\sum_{j\in S_{n+k}\setminus S_n}N_j(\zeta)^2\leq tv_{n+k}$. First choose $k$ large in step 1.2 so that its far negative-energy bound is at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. For this fixed $k$, both boundary-cell counts are $O_k(n^{d-1})$ and $v_{n+k}/v_n\to1$, so choosing $a$ small and then $n$ large makes the near bound at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. The far estimate uses $T_n\leq T_n^h+q^2V_n$ for a fixed $q$ with $h(r)\geq r^2$ when $r\geq q$. Consequently, for each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)\geq-\epsilon T_n^h(\omega)-\epsilon V_n$$
uniformly over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $T_n^h\leq H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+bN$. For each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, step 1.3 therefore gives
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\leq e^{\beta\epsilon V_n}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N$$
and
$$\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N\leq\Xi(2n+1;ze^{\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1-\epsilon)).$$
The inequality is uniform over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$. [F3, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 For the lower bound, restrict interior particles to $\Lambda_{n-k}$, leaving the corridor empty. Choose $k\geq m_0$, so every interior-exterior cell offset is in the far tail. The two-sided estimate of step 1.2 gives
$$|W(\omega,\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n)|\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_{n-k}(\omega)+2^dtV_{n-k}\bigr).$$
With $T_{n-k}\leq T_{n-k}^h+q^2V_{n-k}$, choose $k$ large enough that the right side is at most $\epsilon(T_{n-k}^h+V_n)$. Since $T_{n-k}^h\leq H_{n-k,\mathrm{free}}+bN$, integration over the restricted positions yields
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta\epsilon V_n}\Xi(2(n-k)+1;ze^{-\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1+\epsilon))$$
uniformly over $\zeta$. For fixed $\epsilon$, the selected $k$ is fixed as $n\to\infty$, and the removed corridor volume fraction vanishes. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Divide the bounds in steps 2.1–2.2 by $V_n$ and let $n\to\infty$; [F4] supplies the perturbed free-cube pressure limits. These limits are finite convex functions of $(\beta,\log z)$ by Hölder's inequality [F5], since finite-volume log partition functions are convex and pointwise limits preserve convexity. A finite convex function is continuous on the open parameter domain $\beta>0$, $z>0$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ in both uniform bounds. Their upper and lower limits coincide with $p(z,\beta)$ uniformly over $\Omega(t)$. For $t=0$, every exterior configuration in $\Omega(0)$ is empty, so the equality with the free-wall pressure is immediate. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume superstability and regularity, let $(\Omega_k)$ be van Hove, and let $N_k/|\Omega_k|\to\rho$ for an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Use the general-region free-wall convention of [[thm-tdmath-superstable-van-hove-pressure]], namely
$$Z(\Lambda,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\{q\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)\right)dq_1\cdots dq_N\quad(N\geq1),$$

$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log Z(\Omega_k,N_k;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$

The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp$ is positive and differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log$ is defined on positive reals and $(\log u)'=u'/u$ for differentiable $u>0$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has a point where its secant slope equals its derivative.

[A1] For every compact $K\subset J$ there is a nonnegative summable sequence $(a_i)$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)e^{-\beta E_i}\le a_i$ for all $i$ and $\beta\in K$; the tail $\sum_{i>N}a_i$ tends to zero.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule]]: differentiating $e^{-\beta E_i}$ with respect to $\beta$ uses the one-variable chain rule.

## Proof

**Given:** The countable canonical model and the local summable envelope in the statement.

1.1 On a compact interval $K\subset J$, let $Z_N$, $D_N$, and $Q_N$ be the first $N$ partial sums of $\sum_i g_i e^{-\beta E_i}$, $-\sum_i g_iE_ie^{-\beta E_i}$, and $\sum_i g_iE_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}$. Since $|E_i|^r\le1+|E_i|^2$ for $r=0,1,2$, each tail is bounded uniformly on $K$ by the corresponding tail of $\sum_i a_i$, which tends to zero [A1]. Thus all three sequences converge uniformly; call their limits $Z,D,Q$. Each finite partial sum has the displayed derivatives by the chain rule [F5] and the exponential derivative [F2]. Each partial sum is continuous, so the uniform limits are continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ definition of continuity. [F1, A1, F2, F5]

2.1 For an interior $\beta$ and sufficiently small $h\ne0$, apply [F4] to $Z_N$ on the interval with endpoints $\beta$ and $\beta+h$: its difference quotient is $D_N(\xi_{N,h})$ for some intermediate $\xi_{N,h}$. Choose $N=N(h)$ so that $\sup_K|Z_N-Z|<h^2$ and $\sup_K|D_N-D|<|h|$. The difference quotient for $Z$ then differs from $D(\beta)$ by at most $2|h|+|h|+\sup_{|t-\beta|\le|h|}|D(t)-D(\beta)|$, which tends to zero by continuity of $D$. Hence $Z'=D$. Applying the same argument to $D_N$ and $Q_N$ proves $D'=Q$, so the displayed derivatives hold. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. The envelope also gives $\sum_i p_i|E_i|$ and $\sum_i p_iE_i^2$ finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F3] yields $-Z'/Z=\bar E$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\langle E^2\rangle-\bar E^2=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $p_i/g_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$, its logarithm is $-\beta E_i-\log Z$. The finite first moment makes $\sum_i p_i|\log(p_i/g_i)|\le |\beta|\sum_i p_i|E_i|+|\log Z|\sum_i p_i<\infty$; summing the identity gives $H_g=\beta\bar E+\log Z$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex, let $p\in\mathbb R^d$, and define $g(x)=f(x)-\langle p,x\rangle$. Assume $g$ is **coercive**, meaning that for every $M\in\mathbb R$ there is $R>0$ such that $\|x\|_2\ge R$ implies $g(x)>M$. Then $g$ has a finite global minimum at some $x_*\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The supremum defining $f^*(p)$ is finite and attained at $x_*$, and $p\in\partial f(x_*)$. No uniqueness is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The function conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]], the Fenchel definitions of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]], and the coercivity condition in the Statement.

[L1] [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]]: the epigraph is closed if and only if every weak sublevel set is closed, equivalently if and only if the function is lower semicontinuous.

[L2] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] makes the shear $T(x,r)=(x,r+\langle p,x\rangle)$ linear, and [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]] supplies $K\ge0$ such that $\|Tz-Tz'\|_2\le K\|z-z'\|_2$ for all $z,z'\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$.

[L3] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded Euclidean sets are compact.

[L4] [[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]]: a family of closed subsets of a compact metric space with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection.

[L5] [[thm-infimum-property]] and [[def-infimum]]: every nonempty real set bounded below has an infimum; [[lem-inf-epsilon]] gives a point below $m+\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

[L6] [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]: every nonempty finite set of real numbers has a maximum.

[L7] [[lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality]]: equality in Fenchel's inequality at a finite point is equivalent to the subgradient inequality.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $f$ is proper, choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and put $c=g(x_0)\in\mathbb R$. By coercivity, first choose a radius $R_0>0$ such that $g(x)>c+1$ whenever $\|x\|_2\ge R_0$, then enlarge it to $R>\max\{R_0,\|x_0\|_2\}$; the same implication holds for this $R$. Let $K=\{x:\|x\|_2\le R\}$; it is nonempty, closed, bounded, and therefore compact by [L3]. [given, L3, choose]

1.2 The epigraph of $g$ is $T^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}f)$, because $g(x)\le r$ exactly when $f(x)\le r+\langle p,x\rangle$. By [L1], $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed. Fix $z\notin T^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}f)$; openness of the complement of $\operatorname{epi}f$ gives $\varepsilon>0$ such that the Euclidean ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $Tz$ misses $\operatorname{epi}f$. Set $\rho=\varepsilon/(K+1)>0$. If $\|z'-z\|_2<\rho$, [L2] gives $\|Tz'-Tz\|_2\le K\|z'-z\|_2<\varepsilon$, so $Tz'$ also lies outside $\operatorname{epi}f$. Thus the complement of $T^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}f)$ is open and $\operatorname{epi}g$ is closed. By [L1], $g$ is lower semicontinuous. [L1, L2, given, algebra]

2.1 For each real $r>0$, $U_r=\{x\in K:g(x)>-r\}$ is relatively open in $K$, since its complement is the weak sublevel $K\cap\{g\le-r\}$. These sets cover $K$ because $g(x)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ for every $x$ (properness excludes $-\infty$ and the tilt is finite). Compactness gives a finite subcover, and [L6] supplies a largest real index $r_*$ among its finitely many indices. Since the $U_r$ are nested, $U_{r_*}=K$, so every finite value of $g$ on $K$ is greater than $-r_*$. [L1, L3, L6, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $S:=\{g(x):x\in K,\ g(x)<+\infty\}$. It is nonempty because $x_0\in K$ and $g(x_0)=c$, and it is a real set bounded below by $-r_*$ by step 2.1. It therefore has a real infimum $m$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [L5] gives $s\in S$ with $s<m+\varepsilon$; choosing $x\in K$ with $g(x)=s$ shows $F_\varepsilon:=K\cap\{x:g(x)\le m+\varepsilon\}$ is nonempty. It is closed in $K$ by [L1]. Any nonempty finite subfamily has nonempty intersection, because the member with least positive $\varepsilon$ is contained in all the others; the empty subfamily has intersection $K\ne\emptyset$. [L1, L4, L5, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose]

4.1 Applying [L4] to the family $(F_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ gives $x_*\in\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}F_\varepsilon$. The bound $g(x_*)\le m+1$ makes $g(x_*)$ finite, so $g(x_*)\in S$ and $m\le g(x_*)$. If $g(x_*)>m$, choose $\varepsilon=(g(x_*)-m)/2>0$; then $x_*\in F_\varepsilon$ would give $g(x_*)\le m+\varepsilon<g(x_*)$, a contradiction. Thus $g(x_*)=m$. [L4, step 3.1, algebra, choose]

5.1 For $x\notin K$, step 1.1 gives $g(x)>c+1\ge m+1$, because $x_0\in K$ implies $m\le c$. Thus $x_*$ is a global minimizer over $\mathbb R^d$, and its value $m$ is finite. [step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 On $\operatorname{dom}f$, $-g(x)=\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$, and outside this domain $g(x)=+\infty$. The global minimum $m$ is attained at $x_*\in\operatorname{dom}f$, so the supremum in the definition of $f^*(p)$ is finite, equals $-m$, and is attained at $x_*$. Therefore $f^*(p)=\langle p,x_*\rangle-f(x_*)$; [L7] yields $p\in\partial f(x_*)$. [given, L7, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $f$ be the indicator of $[-1,1]$. The zero tilt $f(y)-0\cdot y$ has every point of the interval as a minimizer, and $f^*(0)=0$ is attained at every such point. Equivalently, $0\in\partial f(x)$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Thus the supporting face at slope zero is the whole interval, and coercive Fenchel attainment need not be unique.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The indicator $f(x)=0$ for $x\in[-1,1]$ and $f(x)=+\infty$ otherwise.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]: the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set is proper, closed, and convex in the given conventions.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]]: $f^*(p)$ is the supremum of $py-f(y)$ over $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and $p\in\partial f(x)$ means $f(y)\ge f(x)+p(y-x)$ for all $y$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]]: a proper indicator with a closed convex epigraph is closed and convex in the local extended-real conventions.

[L1] [[lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality]]: equality in Fenchel's inequality at a finite point is equivalent to the subgradient condition and attainment of the conjugate supremum.

[L2] [[thm-tdmath-fenchel-attainment]]: if the closed proper convex tilt is coercive, it has a finite global minimum and the conjugate supremum is attained, without a uniqueness conclusion.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct calculation.

1.1 The epigraph is $[-1,1]\times[0,\infty)$, a nonempty closed convex rectangle, and the domain $[-1,1]$ is nonempty; hence the indicator is proper, closed, and convex by [F1, F3]. At slope $p=0$, every $y\in[-1,1]$ contributes $0$ to the conjugate supremum, and no other $y$ is in the effective domain, so $f^*(0)=0$ and every point of the interval attains this supremum. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Fix any $x\in[-1,1]$. For every $y\in\mathbb R$, $f(y)\ge0=f(x)+0(y-x)$: equality holds on the interval and the left side is $+\infty$ outside it. Hence $0\in\partial f(x)$; [L1] also gives $f^*(0)=0=0\cdot x-f(x)$ at each such $x$. [F2, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The zero tilt is $g=f$. It is coercive as an extended-real function: for any $M\in\mathbb R$, choosing $R=2$ ensures $|x|\ge R$ implies $g(x)=+\infty>M$. Its minimum is $0$, attained at every $x\in[-1,1]$, so this example satisfies [L2] while exhibiting nonuniqueness and a whole flat supporting face. [L2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and constants $c,\epsilon>0$. Set $p=d+\epsilon$ and
define the even radial pair potential
$$\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(x):=\begin{cases}+\infty,&\|x\|_2<1,\\-c\|x\|_2^{-p},&\|x\|_2\ge1.\end{cases}$$
It has a hard core and a nonzero attractive power tail.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model conventions of
[[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]], $d\ge1$ an integer, and
$c,\epsilon>0$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] defines the pair
energy $U_N$, stability, Euclidean norm, and power-tempering bound.

[F2] [[def-real-power]] and
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] give continuity of positive-base
real powers and $(r^{-p})'=-p r^{-p-1}<0$ for $p>0$. The
[[cor-mean-value-theorem]] therefore makes $r\mapsto r^{-p}$ decreasing on
$(0,\infty)$.

[F3] [[def-integers]]: the number of lattice points
$k\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $\|k\|_\infty=m$ is
$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d$, by subtracting the integer box of radius $m-1$ from the
box of radius $m$.

[F4] [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]] defines the nonnegative series by
its partial sums, and [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] gives
$\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}m^{-1-\epsilon}<\infty$ because $1+\epsilon>1$.

## Verification

1.1 The norm is continuous and $r\mapsto r^{-p}$ is continuous on $r>0$ by
[F2]. The regions $\{\|x\|_2<1\}$ and $\{\|x\|_2\ge1\}$ are Borel, so the
piecewise potential is Borel; radiality makes it even. For $\|x\|_2\ge1$,
$|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(x)|=c\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon}$, so it is power-tempered
with $C=c$ and $R=1$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 Put $\delta:=1/(2\sqrt d)$. For a fixed particle $q_i$, the half-open
cubes $D_k:=q_i+\delta k+[0,\delta)^d$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, partition
$\mathbb R^d$. Their Euclidean diameters are at most $\sqrt d\,\delta=1/2<1$.
The example's definition makes every pair at distance less than $1$ forbidden,
so centers in a finite-energy configuration are separated by at least $1$.
Thus each cube contains at most one center and $D_0$ contains no center other
than $q_i$. The cells in max-norm shell $m$ number
$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d$ by [F3]. For $m\ge1$, factor the difference of powers:
$$(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d=2\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}(2m+1)^{d-1-r}(2m-1)^r\le2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1},$$
since $2m+1\le3m$. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 A neighbor of $q_i$ in shell $m=1$ has distance at least $1$ and
contributes at most $c$ in absolute value; there are $3^d-1$ such cells. For
$m\ge2$, choose a coordinate $r$ with $|k_r|=m$. If $k_r=m$, every point of
$D_k$ differs from $q_i$ in coordinate $r$ by at least $\delta m$; if
$k_r=-m$, the absolute difference is greater than $\delta(m-1)$. Hence every
point of $D_k$ is at Euclidean distance at least $\delta(m-1)$ from $q_i$.
By [F2], each such neighbor contributes at most
$c\delta^{-p}(m-1)^{-p}$. The shell count in step 1.2 therefore bounds its
total contribution by
$$2d3^{d-1}m^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}(m-1)^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
[given, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $m\ge2$, $m-1\ge m/2$, so the last bound is at most

$$\sum_{j\ne i}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|\le C_*:=c(3^d-1)+2d3^{d-1}c\delta^{-p}2^p\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}m^{-1-\epsilon}<\infty.$$
[F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

$$-U_N=\sum_{i<j}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|=\frac12\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}|\phi_{\mathrm{att}}(q_i-q_j)|\le\frac{C_*}{2}N$$

$B=C_*/2$. Together with step 1.1, this proves membership in the stated
